However, when the assumption of stability fails, genuine change in a construct becomes indistinguishable from poor measurement. Conversely, assessing the stability of a construct itself requires a reliable measure. Thus, these two concepts are distinct but mutually dependent and must therefore be evaluated independently. In the case of the truth effect, only when individual differences can be reliably measured and have been established as stable over time, correlations with stable psychological variables can be meaningfully assessed and interpreted.

Reliable Measurement of Individual Differences in the Truth Effect

A few studies have investigated whether individual differences in the truth effect can be reliably measured, with mixed results. One study found only low split-half reliability (Calio et al., 2025), whereas another reported sufficiently high reliability using five experimental sessions, leading the authors to conclude that multiple sessions may be necessary to obtain reliable individual estimates (De Keersmaecker et al., 2026). Unlike standardized psychometric instruments, however, experimental tasks are not fixed.

Truth-effect experiments vary considerably in, for example, stimulus material, instructions, and trial size (i.e., the number of trials per condition, that is, repeated and new trials, respectively). All of these affect reliability (Green et al., 2016), complicating straightforward comparisons and portability of reliability coefficients across studies (Rouder & Haaf, 2019).

Therefore, the role of reliability in experiments has received increasing attention (e.g., Rouder & Haaf, 2019; Rouder & Mehrvarz, 2024; Rouder, Mehrvarz, & Schnuerch, 2026; Rouder et al., 2023) and a different framework for understanding psychometric goodness and reliability in individual differences research in experimental tasks has been developed. Specifically, Rouder et al. (2023) argued that reliability coefficients obtained in a single study are a poor basis for evaluating the psychometric goodness of an experimental task, as reliability depends heavily on trial size-a quantity that varies widely across experimental studies. To address this, these authors proposed the signal-to-noise ratio γ, which captures the psychometric goodness of a task independent of trial size, and from which the expected reliability can be derived for any given number of trials. Building on this framework, Zajdler and Schnuerch (2026) assessed signal-to-noise ratios, trial size, and expected reliability across a wide range of truth effect studies, showing that reliable measurement of individual differences is possible with a manageable number of trials. Moreover, they provided concrete design recommendations for truth-effect experiments to achieve higher task goodness. These recommendations include, for example, having a sample from the general population and using unknown trivia statements as stimulus material. In addition, the authors emphasize the critical role of trial size to ensure sufficient reliability.

Stability of Individual Differences in the Truth Effect

The temporal stability of individual differences in the truth effect is often implicitly assumed. Researchers studying how individual truth effects relate to personality traits or cognitive abilities typically administer the paradigm once and treat the resulting scores as a measure of a stable, underlying disposition. This assumption may be sensible: several judgment and decision-making phenomena have been found to be stable within individuals.

For instance, individual differences in delay discounting are stable for up to one year and across a range of stimulus materials (Odum, 2011), differences in the acquiescence bias are stable over time and generalize across tests (Couch & Keniston, 1960), and response biases in recognition memory are stable across time, presentation modes, and stimulus materials (Kantner & Lindsay, 2012 , 2014). Similarly, individual differences in the recognition heuristic have been shown to be stable across time, presentation modes, and domains (Michalkiewicz & Erdfelder, 2016). Given the evidence for these other judgment phenomena, it is reasonable to assume stable individual differences in the truth effect as well-however, it is an empirical question that warrants its own investigation.

As a first step to directly address this, Calio et al. (2025) examined the test-retest stability of individual differences in the truth effect across two sessions set one week apart. They found only low and often non-significant correlations, though the authors acknowledged that these results may reflect insufficient reliability of the employed measures, rather than genuine instability. De Keersmaecker et al. (2026) further assessed the stability of individual differences in the truth effect by measuring individual differences across five sessions spaced roughly one week apart. They used the full five sessions to estimate a stable component and found remarkably high stability of individual differences.

In both studies, temporal stability was assessed in a test-retest design. This, however, is only one aspect of temporal stability, which may also include the stability of individual differences across different retention intervals, not just sessions. Thus, the evidence here is limited and not without ambiguity, and therefore warrants further investigation across broader conditions.

The Present Research

Taken together, important steps have been undertaken to establish the prerequisites of reliability and stability necessary for more grounded research on individual differences in the truth effect and their correlates. Yet, two open questions remain. First, while Zajdler and Schnuerch (2026) suggest that the truth effect can be reliably measured within a single session-provided sufficient psychometric goodness and trial size-these recommendations were derived retrospectively from existing studies and have not yet been validated in a study designed to follow them deliberately. Second, because prior research has relied on the same experimental procedure repeated across multiple sessions (Calio et al., 2025; De Keersmaecker et al., 2026), it remains unclear whether individual differences in the truth effect are stable not only across sessions, but across different retention intervals as well.

The present research aims to address these aspects. We first reanalyze three existing datasets, spanning different designs, session numbers, and retention intervals, to assess whether we can detect and reproduce the existing evidence for temporal stability of individual differences-in some datasets under conditions not optimized for this purpose.

To do so, we specify a Bayesian hierarchical model explicitly modeling the correlation structure of individual truth effects across measurement occasions. The Bayesian approach allows us to quantify uncertainty in our correlation estimates more rigorously than conventional methods and to directly test the null hypothesis that there is no stability in individual differences. We then report a new, preregistered experiment, designed in accordance with Zajdler and Schnuerch's (2026) recommendations, that expands prior work on the stability over different retention intervals. Participants completed the same truth-effect procedure with a short retention phase across two sessions; critically, at the second session, participants additionally judged statements from the first session's exposure phase. This allowed us to assess the stability of individual differences not only between sessions but also across different retention interval lengths within the same design.

To foreshadow our results, across both the reanalyses and our experiment, we find relatively high correlations between individual truth effects across sessions and retention intervals in data with acceptable reliability. Together, these results validate the existing design recommendations, demonstrate that reliable measurement is achievable within a single session, and provide broader evidence for the temporal stability of individual differences in the truth effect. Thus, we establish the prerequisites for meaningfully assessing how individual differences in the truth effect relate to dispositional variables.

Datasets and Analytical Approach Datasets

We first reanalyzed three publicly available datasets from previous studies on the temporal stability of the truth effect. We chose these datasets because these are, to our knowledge, the only openly available datasets explicitly examining the stability of the truth effect across time, either at the individual level or on average. Two datasets investigated the stability of individual differences in the truth effect across multiple sessions (Datasets 1 and 2), and one examined how the average truth effect changes across different retention intervals in a within-participant design (Dataset 3). All data are available on the Open Science Framework (OSF).foot_0 Lastly, a fourth dataset is from our own preregistered experiment (https://osf.io/kg75p). An overview of sample and study characteristics of all datasets is provided in Table 1; more detailed descriptions of each follow in the respective sections below.

Prior to analysis, we rescaled truth judgments to range from -1 ("definitely false") to +1 ("definitely true") to ensure comparability between studies. On this scale, individual truth effects can range from -2 to 2, where 0 indicates no truth effect, 2 indicates that all repeated statements were rated as definitely true and all novel statements as definitely false, and -2 indicates a perfect reversal of this pattern.

The Signal-to-Noise Ratio γ and Reliability

For each study, we report the signal-to-noise ratio γ = σ B /σ W (Rouder & Mehrvarz, 2024; Rouder et al., 2023) and the expected reliability at the implemented trial size as measures of psychometric goodness for each session. The signal-to-noise ratio γ is the ratio of between-person variability in individual truth effects, σ B (the signal), to within-person trial-level variability, σ W (the noise). Its relationship to reliability is given by where L denotes the number of trials per condition (the trial size).

To estimate γ, we used the Bayesian hierarchical model of Zajdler and Schnuerch (2026). The expected reliability for each session is then obtained by substituting the posterior mean of γ and the trial size L into the above equation.

Statistical Model

The central substantive question concerns the temporal stability of individual differences in the truth effect. To that end, we implement the competing theoretical positions as statistical models and then compare them by means of Bayes factor. We begin with the trial-level observation model, on which we then build the different models of stability. In a truth effect experiment, each participant i completes ℓ truth judgments for repeated and novel statements, respectively. Let Y ijkℓ denote the ith (i = 1, . . . , I) individual's truth judgment for the ℓth statement (l = 1, . . . , L jk ) in the jth test (j = 1, . . . , J) and the kth condition (k = 1, 2, for repeated versus novel statements).

We place the following linear model on Y ijkℓ (Schnuerch et al., 2021): where α ij is the person-by-test-specific intercept, that is, the general tendency of participant i to judge any statement at test j as true, regardless of condition.

The term β i represents the person-specific influence of factual truth on truth judgments, where T jℓ codes the truth status of the ℓth statement at the jth test. It takes the value -0.5 for false statements or 0.5 for true statements. The parameters of interest, the person-and test-specific truth effects, are denoted as θ ij . Here, X k denotes the repetition condition and is coded as -0.5 (if the statement is novel) or 0.5 (if it is repeated). The term τ² denotes the unsystematic variance of the observed values, that is, trial-by-trial noise.

Let θ i = (θ i1 , . . . , θ iJ ) denote each participant's individual truth effects across all J tests. We place the following multivariate model on θ i : with µ = (µ 1 , . . . , µ J ) denoting the test-specific means across participants.

The variance-covariance matrix Σ is constructed as where D(σ) is a diagonal matrix with test-specific systematic standard deviations σ = (σ 1 , . . . , σ J ) and Ω is the correlation matrix.

Models on Ω

The theoretical positions on the stability of individual differences in the truth effect are represented by different statistical models placed on the correlation matrix Ω.

No Stability of Individual Differences in the Truth Effect.

This model, denoted as M 0 , represents the notion that individual differences in the truth effect are not stable, that is, unrelated across tests. The correlation matrix Ω is therefore modeled as the identity matrix, such that correlations between different tests are zero:

Stability of Individual Differences in the Truth Effect.

Model M 1 , in contrast, is a flexible model, where the correlations of individual truth effects between the different tests are freely estimated. It thereby represents the expectation that individual truth effects do covary across tests. We place an LKJ prior on Ω, Ω ∼ LKJ(η), with the shape parameter set to η = 1. This choice corresponds to a weakly informative prior that assigns equal prior weight to all valid correlation matrices and thus does not favor any particular correlation structure. Compared to alternative priors on the covariance structure, such as the Inverse-Wishart distribution, the LKJ prior is computationally less efficient but yields more accurate estimates (Yang & Rouder, 2026).

Prior Specification

Model specification is completed by defining priors on all model parameters. We specify priors on the group-level parameters characterizing the truth effects, θ, as following the reasoning by Schnuerch et al. (2021) and Schnuerch and Rouder (2026).

These priors are consistent with typical effect sizes reported in the literature, and the half-normal on σ j ensures strictly positive variance parameters. Priors on all remaining parameters are set to be weakly informative; full details are provided in Appendix A.

Sensitivity Analysis

Prior specification is an inherently subjective component of Bayesian analysis.

While this allows prior knowledge to be formally incorporated into the analysis, it also introduces the risk that results are sensitive to the particular priors chosen. It is therefore common practice to assess the robustness of Bayesian results across a range of reasonable prior settings. To assess the sensitivity of our results to prior specification for µ j , σ j , and Ω, we repeated all following model-based analyses with alternative prior settings.

Specifically, we varied the mean of the prior on µ j across {0.125; 0.25; 0.5}, the scale of the prior on σ j across {0.125; 0.25; 0.5}, and the LKJ shape parameter η across {0.5; 1; 2}. The choice of prior did not meaningfully change any results. Full details of the sensitivity analyses are provided in Appendix B.

Model Comparison

To compare the statistical models outlined above, we use Bayes factors (Jeffreys, 1961). The Bayes factor is defined as and quantifies the relative strength of evidence for one model (M 1 ) over another (M 0 ) by comparing how well each predicts the observed data (Kass & Raftery, 1995; Rouder & Morey, 2019).

Crucially, more flexible models, that is, models imposing fewer restrictions on the structure of individual differences, make more diffuse predictions and are therefore penalized for their flexibility. This makes Bayes factors a natural tool for model comparison in the present context, where we wish to decide between models that differ in the constraints they place on the correlation structure of individual differences.

Computing Bayes factors requires evaluating the marginal likelihood p(data|M) for each model, a high-dimensional integral that is analytically intractable particularly in hierarchical models. We therefore estimate Bayes factors via bridge sampling, an efficient sampling-based integration method that is well-suited to the hierarchical models employed here (Gronau et al., 2017).

Bayes factors are interpreted continuously, but there are conventional benchmarks for its interpretation (e.g. Jeffreys, 1961; Kass & Raftery, 1995). Values between 1 and 3 are considered anecdotal evidence and barely worth mentioning; values between 3 and 10 indicate substantial evidence, and values between 10 and 100 indicate strong evidence. A Bayes Factor larger than 100 is considered decisive or very strong evidence.

Software and Estimation

All analyses were conducted in R (R Core Team, 2026). We obtained posterior distributions for all parameters by Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) sampling in Stan (Stan Development Team, 2026a, 2026b) through the rstan package (Stan Development Team, 2025). Bayes factors for model comparisons were computed with the bridgesampling package (Gronau et al., 2020). Visualizations were created with ggplot2 (Wickham, 2016). Code to reproduce all analyses and tables is available on the OSF (https://osf.io/kg75p).

We ran 12 chains with 5,000 post-warmup samples each (warmup = 1,000), resulting in 60,000 posterior samples per parameter. Model convergence was assessed by inspecting MCMC chains and computing R convergence statistics, all of which were below 1.01. Effective sample sizes were satisfactory for all critical parameters. For each dataset, MCMC diagnostics are reported alongside posterior means and standard deviations of central parameters in Appendix C.

Dataset 1 Dataset

This dataset is from Experiment 1 in Calio et al. (2025) who investigated the reliability and test-retest stability of individual differences in the truth effect. In a two-part online study, participants performed two identically constructed truth-effect experiments spaced approximately one week apart. In the exposure phase of each session, participants sorted 32 statements into semantic categories. After completing a 10-minute non-verbal filler task, participants moved on to the judgment phase, where they provided truth judgments on a scale from 1 ("definitely false") to 6 ("definitely true") for 20 repeated and 20 novel statements. This procedure was repeated one week later using a new set of statements. On average, repeated statements were assigned higher truth judgments than novel statements, both in Session 1, M rep -M new = 0.07 (SD = 0.17), t(165) = 5.63, p < .001, Cohen's d = 0.44, and Session 2, M rep -M new = 0.07 (SD = 0.17), t(165) = 5.32, p < .001, Cohen's d = 0.41. However, the authors found no evidence of test-retest stability of individual differences in the truth effect across the two sessions, and attributed this to low reliability.

Results

Psychometric Properties and Pearson Correlations

The signal-to-noise ratio for Dataset 1 was γ1 = 0.05, 95%-credible interval This means that trial-by-trial noise was 14 to 20 times higher than systematic variability, indicating rather low psychometric goodness for measuring individual differences. The study had L = 20 trials per condition at each session, yielding low expected reliability of individual truth effects of ρ1 = .03 in Session 1 and ρ2 = .05 in Session 2. For reference, an expected reliability of ρ = .80 would have required L ≥ 1,600 trials per condition.

The Pearson correlation between the observed individual truth effects (i.e., difference scores, M rep -M new ) in the two test sessions was r = .04, 95%-confidence interval [-0.11, 0.19], t(164) = 0.55, p = .58, suggesting that individual differences in the truth effect are not stable over time.

Discussion

We find no support for one model over the other in this dataset. Consistent with the low signal-to-noise ratio and low reliability documented above, the very broad credible interval and the inconclusive Bayes factor together support the conclusion that these data are too noisy to draw meaningful conclusions about the stability of individual differences in the truth effect. This largely replicates the non-significant test-retest stability findings of Calio et al. (2025), who themselves suspected that low reliability rather than a true absence of stable individual differences may have been responsible.

Our results provide further evidence that with low signal-to-noise ratio, not even hierarchical modeling is effective in localizing correlations (Rouder et al., 2023). What Bayesian hierarchical modeling does offer, however, is an honest accounting of uncertainty (see also Rouder, Yang, & Braver, 2026). Rather than a non-significant point estimate that might be misread as evidence for the null, Bayesian hierarchical approaches allow us to obtain a credible interval that makes visible how little the data can tell us. We therefore do not conclude that individual differences in the truth effect are unstable, only that these -0.5 0.0 0.5 -0.5 0.0 0.5 Session 1 Session 2 Model Observed 0.00 0.25 0.50 0.75 1.00 -1.0 -0.5 0.0 0.5 1.0 Correlation Density Note. data are too noisy to arbitrate the question. Overall, these results reinforce the importance of reliability and careful experimental design when studying individual differences (e.g., Rouder, Mehrvarz, & Schnuerch, 2026; Zajdler & Schnuerch, 2026).

In Dataset 2, we turn to a study that found evidence for both reliability and stability of individual differences in the truth effect. A critical difference from the Calio et al. (2025) data is that this study employed more sessions and used hierarchical modeling. Our aim is to reproduce these findings with our modeling approach and extend them by testing the correlations via Bayes factor. This can extend the evidence for stability of individual differences over time by demonstrating its analytical robustness (see e.g., Aczel et al., 2026).

Results

Psychometric Properties and Pearson Correlations

The signal-to-noise ratio for Dataset 2 was good across all sessions, ranging from γ = 0.56, indicating that systematic variability is about half as large as the trial-by-trial noise, to γ = 0.69, where systematic variability is about two thirds of the noise. Based on these estimates and L = 20 trials per condition, a reliability of individual truth effects between ρ = .76 and ρ = .83 would be expected across sessions.

Table 2 displays the signal-to-noise ratio and corresponding expected reliability for each session alongside pairwise Pearson correlations.

Pearson correlations of individual observed truth-effect difference scores (i.e., M rep -M new ) across sessions ranged from r = .47 to r = .72, and did not appear to decline systematically between sessions with longer spacing in-between (Table 2). Overall, this is a first indication that individual differences in the truth effect are stable over time: reliability was reasonably high, and correlations were-if anything-attenuated rather than inflated by measurement error (e.g., Rouder, Mehrvarz, & Schnuerch, 2026), meaning the true stability of individual differences in the truth effect is likely at least as strong as these correlations suggest.

Model-Based Results

Reanalyzing the data with the Bayesian hierarchical model, the posterior estimates of the correlations between sessions ranged from r = .52 to r = .88. Note that because the factual truth status of statements was not available for this dataset, we could not include the predictor β (which captures the influence of factual truth on truth judgments) in the model.

Discussion

These findings reproduce those of the original authors and strongly support the conclusion that individual differences in the truth effect are stable across sessions. A small difference is that, while we still find high correlations across sessions with our model, our model-based correlation estimates are somewhat lower than theirs. Moreover, rather than explicitly estimating a full correlation matrix as we do here, they computed Pearson correlations on model-estimated individual truth-effect scores. Both of these differences can be expected to yield somewhat different correlation estimates. The substantive conclusion, however, remains the same.

It is also worth revisiting reliability in light of these results. Although both this dataset and Dataset 1 had the same trial size, reliability is consistently higher here, due to a higher signal-to-noise ratio γ across sessions. De Keersmaecker et al. ( 2026) used all five sessions jointly to estimate reliability of individual truth effects and concluded that this many sessions may be necessary to achieve satisfactory reliability. By instead estimating γ and reliability separately for each session, we show that reliability is already satisfactory within single sessions. This suggests that the higher reliability achieved here relative to Dataset 1 is not primarily a function of using five sessions per se, but more plausibly reflects the higher per-session γ in this dataset.

Moreover, we find evidence for the stability of individual differences in the truth effect, both using the hierarchical model and Pearson correlations of observed truth-effect scores. As expected, the Pearson correlations are attenuated relative to the model-based estimates, yet remain well detectable and clearly different from zero. That the difference between the model-based estimates and the Pearson correlations is not too large reflects the higher reliability in this dataset. It should be noted that, opposed to simply correlating values from each session, where each correlation is only informed by answers given in these sessions, our hierarchical approach takes into account all sessions-as did De Keersmaecker et al. (2026) in their original approach.

Taken together, these results provide further evidence that individual differences in the truth effect are stable across occasions. One aim of this research, however, is to establish temporal stability in a broader sense. Therefore, we also want to assess whether stability holds across different retention intervals-a question that the first two datasets, with only short, same-session retention intervals, did not address. Thus, before turning to our own experiment, we consider another study that speaks to the stability of individual differences across varying retention intervals.

Dataset 3 Dataset

Dataset 3 comes from Henderson et al. (2021) who studied how the average size of the truth effect behaves across different retention intervals with the same participants.

Even though these data were not designed to capture individual truth effects, they may still contain information about the stability of individual differences in the truth effect across different retention intervals.

The online study consisted of four sessions. In the first session, participants sorted 64 statements into different semantic categories. They then immediately completed the first judgment phase where they judged the truth of 16 repeated and 16 novel statements on a scale from 1 ("definitely false") to 7 ("definitely true"). The following sessions consisted only of a judgment phase, where participants judged the truth of 16 repeated and 16 novel statements on the same 7-point scale. These sessions took place one day after the exposure phase, one week after the exposure phase, and one month after the exposure phase.

Even though the average effect decreased with each session, the truth effect was present in all four sessions: repeated statements consistently received higher truth judgments than novel statements, immediately after exposure, M rep -M new = 0.22 (SD = 0.29), t(514) = 17.83, p < .001, Cohen's d = 0.79, after one day, M rep -M new = 0.13 (SD = 0.20), t(514) = 14.54, p < .001, Cohen's d = 0.64, after one week, M rep -M new = 0.09 (SD = 0.16), t(514) = 12.82, p < .001, Cohen's d = 0.57, and after one month, M rep -M new = 0.05 (SD = 0.15), t(514) = 7.64, p < .001, Cohen's d = 0.34.

Results

Psychometric Properties and Pearson Correlations

The signal-to-noise ratio for Dataset 3 decreased from session to session with longer retention intervals, ranging from γ = 0.04, indicating that the trial-by-trial noise is about 25 times larger than systematic variability, to γ = 0.54, where systematic variability is about half as large as the noise. Based on these estimates and L = 16 trials per condition, a reliability of individual truth effects between ρ = .01 and ρ = .70 would be expected across sessions. Table 4 presents the signal-to-noise ratio and corresponding expected reliability for each session alongside pairwise Pearson correlations.

Pearson correlations of individual observed truth-effect scores (i.e., M rep -M new ) across sessions ranged from r = .03 to r = .36 (Table 4).

Many correlations are non-significant and confidence intervals often span zero, suggesting there is no stability of individual differences across different retention intervals. However, as psychometric goodness and reliability are rather low in most cases, these values should not be over-interpreted.

Model-Based Results

The reanalysis with the Bayesian hierarchical model yielded posterior estimates of the correlations between sessions from .28 to .67, with the highest correlation observed between Session 1 (immediately after exposure) and Session 2 (one day after exposure), and the lowest between Session 3 (one week after exposure) and Session 4 (one month after exposure). Table 5 displays all posterior means for the correlations alongside their 95%-credible intervals, which are wide and often span zero. Model comparison via Bayes factor was not possible for this dataset, as bridge sampling failed to converge despite a well-behaved posterior (all R < 1.01, no divergent transitions). 2 2 We suspected that this may be because the estimated between-person variance of the truth effect in the last session was close to zero, that is, close to a boundary of the parameter space.

We therefore re-estimated the model using only the first three sessions. Parameter estimates were similar for the threeand four-session models (see Tables C3 and C4 in Appendix C). Bayes Factor model comparison decisively favored M 1 over M 0 , BF10 = 1.68 × 10 24 , suggesting that individual differences in the truth effect covary across different retention intervals.

Discussion

These findings support the conclusion that individual differences in the truth effect are stable across different retention intervals, as the model detected substantial correlations -0.4 0.0 0.4 0.8 1.2 -0.4 0.0 0.4 0.8 1.2 Session 1 Session 2 0 2 4 6 8 -1.0 -0.5 0.0 0.5 1.0 Correlation Density -0.4 0.0 0.4 0.8 1.2 -0.4 0.0 0.4 0.8 1.2 Session 1 Session 3 0 2 4 6 8 -1.0 -0.5 0.0 0.5 1.0 Correlation Density -0.4 0.0 0.4 0.8 1.2 -0.4 0.0 0.4 0.8 1.2 Session 1 Session 4 0 2 4 6 8 -1.0 -0.5 0.0 0.5 1.0 Correlation Density -0.4 0.0 0.4 0.8 1.2 -0.4 0.0 0.4 0.8 1.2 Session 2 Session 3 0 2 4 6 8 -1.0 -0.5 0.0 0.5 1.0 Correlation Density -0.4 0.0 0.4 0.8 1.2 -0.4 0.0 0.4 0.8 1.2 Session 2 Session 4 0 2 4 6 8 -1.0 -0.5 0.0 0.5 1.0 Correlation Density -0.4 0.0 0.4 0.8 1.2 -0.4 0.0 0.4 0.8 1.2 Session 3 Session 4 Model Observed 0 2 4 6 8 -1.0 -0.5 0.0 0.5 1.0 Correlation Density Note. The left column displays individual observed (gray) and model-estimated (blue) truth effects for each of the session pairs in Dataset 3. The right column shows the posterior distributions of the correlations (histograms); the dashed blue line marks the posterior means, and the red dot indicates the Pearson correlation point estimates with the corresponding confidence intervals. Some posterior distributions are rather narrow, while others span a broader interval, reflecting the variable psychometric properties across sessions.

across different retention intervals. Even though the average truth effect decreased with longer intervals, individuals who showed larger truth effects immediately after exposure also tended to show larger truth effects after one month.

It should be noted that, nonetheless, there is still considerable uncertainty about the extent to which individual differences are associated across different retention intervals.

This is reflected both in the low signal-to-noise ratios and reliability estimates and in the wide posterior distributions and credible intervals of the correlation estimates. Notably, signal-to-noise ratios decreased with longer retention intervals-a pattern that, combined with the generally low trial size, resulted in lower reliability for these longer retention intervals. That the hierarchical model nevertheless identified substantial covariation speaks to one of its key advantages over simple Pearson correlations: rather than estimating each pairwise correlation in isolation, the model draws on data from all sessions simultaneously when estimating the full correlation matrix. Still, the wide posterior distributions for some correlation estimates signal that the data are, at least in part, too noisy for precise estimation.

Our own new experiment, presented next, now aims to replicate this general pattern of stability, both across sessions and retention intervals, under conditions of higher reliability and within one study. To that end, we deliberately followed Zajdler and Schnuerch's (2026) experimental design recommendations and combined them with a high trial size in order to achieve reliable measurement of individual differences within a single session. We were able to simultaneously examine the stability of individual differences across different sessions and retention intervals by having participants judge statements from both the first and the second sessions' exposure phases at the second session.

Together, this allows us to demonstrate that reliable measurement of individual differences in the truth effect is achievable in a single session, and to provide more definitive evidence for their stability, both across sessions and retention intervals.

Experiment Method

We designed the experiment in accordance with the recommendations derived in prior work (Zajdler & Schnuerch, 2026). Specifically, we used interest ratings in the exposure phase and filled the short retention intervals with a demanding numerical distractor task rather than a questionnaire. The stimuli were unknown trivia statements, and the study was deployed online targeting a general population sample rather than a student sample. In line with the recommendations, we employed short, same-session retention intervals. The one-week interval between sessions also served as a longer retention interval, motivated by our substantive interest in whether individual differences in the truth effect remain stable over longer intervals as well.

The study design and analysis plan were preregistered (https://osf.io/thsep) and all data, study materials, and analysis scripts are openly available on the OSF (https://osf.io/kg75p).

Design

The experiment had a 2 × 2 × 3 within-subjects design. The three within-subjects factors were item repetition (repeated vs. novel), factual truth (true vs. false), and retention interval of the repeated statements (Test 1: short delay within Session 1, Test 2: short delay within Session 2, and Test 3: one-week delay between Session 1 and Session 2).

The experiment consisted of two sessions, one week apart. Each session had three phases: an exposure phase, where statements were presented and rated for interest; a brief retention phase involving an unrelated filler task; and a judgment phase, where participants made truth judgments for both repeated and novel statements. The full procedure is described in detail below.

Material

We determined the required number of statements based on the signal-to-noise ratio framework outlined above. For studies in line with Zajdler and Schnuerch's (2026) recommendations, γ typically ranged between 0.6 and 0.7. Assuming a γ in this range and aiming for a reliability of ρ ≈ .90, solving results in 50 statements per condition in each of the judgment phases.

Given the design of the present study (see below), this resulted in a total of 300 different statements across both sessions.

Statements were selected to be largely unknown to participants based on norming data and were drawn from statement pools used in previous research. Specifically, we used the 100 difficult statements from Brashier et al. (2020), the 128 statements used by Henderson et al. (2021), and 60 statements that were normed on a binary scale (0 = false,1 = true) by Jalbert et al. (2019) with mean "true" ratings between .4 and .6 to ensure maximum ambiguity. To reach the target of 300 statements, we additionally converted 12 items from the general-knowledge norms of Tauber et al. (2013) into true/false statement format. To match the difficulty of the other statements, we selected items that had been answered correctly by fewer than 5% of norming participants. This completed our pool of 300 statements (150 false, 150 true). We additionally included four obviously true or false items that served as attention checks (e.g., "One day has 24 hours.", see Nadarevic et al., 2018). Two of these items appeared in Session 1 and two in Session 2.

For each participant, all statements were randomly assigned to exposure and judgment phases across the experiment by the experimental software, while ensuring that half of the statements were true and half were false in each phase. Moreover, it was ensured that repeated statements were seen exactly twice: once during an exposure phase and once during a judgment phase. For statements from Session 1's exposure phase, this judgment occurred either within the same session (short retention interval) or one week later in Session 2 (long retention interval); for statements from Session 2's exposure phase, the judgment always occurred within the same session (second short retention interval).

Procedure

The experiment comprised two sessions, completed seven to nine days apart. Both sessions consisted of an exposure phase, a short retention interval, and a truth judgment phase.

Session 1. In the exposure phase, participants saw 100 statements (50 true, 50 false), sampled randomly for each participant, and rated each statement for interest on a scale from 1 ("not interesting at all") to 6 ("very interesting"). Participants were not informed of the statements' veracity during the exposure phase or any of the subsequent experimental phases. Following the exposure phase, participants completed a short distractor task in which they judged the correctness of 25 algebraic equations, receiving feedback after each trial. In the subsequent judgment phase, participants judged the truth of 100 statements on a scale from 1 ("definitely false") to 6 ("definitely true"). Of these, 50 statements had been presented during the exposure phase (repeated statements) and 50 were novel. Two common-knowledge control items were additionally included as attention checks. After the judgment phase, we asked participants whether they had worked on the task conscientiously, and they were informed that an honest answer would not affect their compensation. At the end of the session, participants were thanked for their participation and reminded to return for Session 2 one week later. They were contacted through the recruitment platform after seven days as a reminder to complete Session 2. Session 2. Session 2 followed the same general structure as Session 1. In the exposure phase, participants viewed 100 statements (50 true, 50 false) that had not appeared in any phase of Session 1, and again rated each for interest on the same 6-point scale. Participants then completed the same filler task, judging the correctness of 25 algebraic equations. In the judgment phase, participants judged the truth of 150 statements on the same scale ranging from 1 ("definitely false") to 6 ("definitely true"). Of these, 50 statements were from the exposure phase of Session 2, 50 were from the exposure phase of Session 1 (and had not been presented during the Session 1 judgment phase), and 50 were novel. As in Session 1, two common-knowledge control items served as attention checks. At the end of Session 2, participants completed self-report items assessing whether they had used any external resources to judge the statements' truth, either during the study or between sessions, and whether they had worked conscientiously on all tasks. To detect potential use of AI-based response agents, participants were also asked to type (rather than paste) a brief response describing what they believed the goal of the study to be. Finally, participants were thanked for their participation and given the option to learn more about the study's purpose.

Participants

Participants were recruited through the online recruitment platform Connect by CloudResearch (Hartman et al., 2023). They received $5.00 for participation in the first session (approximately 25 minutes) and an additional $8.00 for participation in the second session (approximately 35 minutes). Eligibility required that participants be at least 18 years old and native English speakers residing in the United States, as the statement material had been normed primarily on U.S. participants.

We initially aimed to recruit 250 participants for Session 1; as no formal power analysis is available for the hierarchical models employed here, the target sample size was determined by financial constraints. Of the initial sample, 30 participants were excluded based on preregistered criteria (e.g., failed attention checks), and were not permitted to return for Session 2. We recruited additional participants to replace them and reach the preregistered target of 250 participants at Session 1. This resulted in a total of 280 participants who completed Session 1, of which 244 were eligible to return for Session 2 after the same exclusion criteria were applied. Of these, 228 participants completed Session 2. Participants who terminated a session early, or who completed only Session 1 without returning for Session 2, were excluded from all analyses.

Among those who completed both sessions, we excluded another 32 participants following our preregistered exclusion criteria. As some participants met more than one criterion, we report exclusions in order of application, and participants are counted toward the first criterion they met. The experimental software recorded how often participants changed the browser window during the judgment phase. To ensure participants did not look up information about the statements' truth while working on the task, participants with more than three such changes were excluded, which applied to 20 participants. To detect potential use of AI-based response agents, participants were required to type a brief response describing what they believed the study goal to be; one participant who pasted text into this field was excluded. We then excluded three participants who indicated, on the respective self-report items, that they had used external help to judge the statements' truth during or between sessions, or that they had not worked on the task conscientiously. We further excluded three participants who provided an incorrect response to more than one of the four attention check items. A response was classified as incorrect with a rating larger than 2 for false statements, or smaller than 5 for true statements on the 6-point scale. One additional participant was excluded due to a software malfunction, and four participants were excluded because they indicated that English was not their native language. This resulted in a final sample of N = 196. Age ranged from 18 to 75 years (M = 38.1, SD = 11.39) and the sample consisted of 108 male (55.1%), 84 female (42.9%), and 4 non-binary (2.0%) participants.

Results

Consistent with other findings, the average magnitude of the truth effect decreased both with repeated testing (De Keersmaecker et al., 2026), that is, from Session 1 with a short retention interval (Test 1) to Session 2 with a short retention interval (Test 2), and after the longer retention interval (Test 3; Henderson et al., 2021). Yet repeated statements were consistently assigned higher truth judgments than novel statements across all three tests: after a short retention interval in Session 1, M rep -M new = 0.37 (SD = 0.36), t(195) = 14.48, p < .001, Cohen's d = 1.03, after a short retention interval in Session 2, M rep -M new = 0.26 (SD = 0.28), t(195) = 12.80, p < .001, Cohen's d = 0.91, and after a one-week retention interval in Session 2, M rep -M new = 0.13 (SD = 0.15), t(195) = 11.51, p < .001, Cohen's d = 0.82.

Psychometric Properties and Pearson Correlations

The signal-to-noise ratio also decreased from session to session and with the longer retention interval, ranging from γ = 0.18 after the one-week retention interval, where the trial-by-trial noise is about 5 times larger than systematic variability, to γ = 0.70 after the short retention interval in Session 1, where systematic variability is about two thirds of the size of the noise.

Based on these estimates, the expected reliability differed considerably across tests.

For Test 1, with L = 50 trials per condition, expected reliability was ρ = .92. For Tests 2 and 3, we calculated reliability at L = 37.5: because the 50 new statements in Session 2 served as novel items in both Test 2 and Test 3, we split them into two random subgroups to avoid artificially inflating the systematic variance. The expected reliability was then ρ = .85 for Test 2, but only ρ = .39 for Test 3, reflecting the considerably lower signal-to-noise ratio after the one-week retention interval. Table 6 displays the signal-to-noise ratio and corresponding expected reliability for each test alongside pairwise Pearson correlations.

Pearson correlations of individual observed truth-effect difference scores (i.e., M rep -M new ) across tests ranged from r = .40 to r = .67. Despite the low reliability associated with Test 3, correlations involving this test are well localized, though expectedly lower (i.e., more attenuated) than those between the two short-retention tests. This replicates the general pattern of stability reported above and provides further evidence that individual differences in the truth effect are stable both across different sessions and retention intervals.

Model-Based Results

Analyzing the data with the Bayesian hierarchical model, the posterior estimates of the correlations between sessions and retention intervals ranged from r = .71 to r = .75.

Table 7 displays all posterior means for the correlations along their 95%-credible intervals and Figure 7 scores, but the difference is small. This reflects the higher reliability from these data on the individual level. For Test 3, however, there is considerably more shrinkage.

Model-estimated effects are pulled more toward the group mean, consistent with the lower reliability associated with the one-week retention interval.

Model comparison via Bayes factors decisively favored M 1 over M 0 , BF10 = 1.57 × 10 34 , indicating that individual differences in the truth effect covary substantially across different sessions and retention intervals. -0.6 -0.2 0.2 0.6 1.0 1.4 -0.6 -0.2 0.2 0.6 1.0 1.4 Test 1 Test 2 0 2 4 6 8 10 -1.0 -0.5 0.0 0.5 1.0 Correlation Density -0.6 -0.2 0.2 0.6 1.0 1.4 -0.6 -0.2 0.2 0.6 1.0 1.4 Test 1 Test 3 Model Observed 0 2 4 6 8 10 -1.0 -0.5 0.0 0.5 1.0 Correlation Density -0.6 -0.2 0.2 0.6 1.0 1.4 -0.6 -0.2 0.2 0.6 1.0 1.4 Test 2 Test 3 0 2 4 6 8 10 -1.0 -0.5 0.0 0.5 1.0 Correlation Density Note. Discussion

The results of our new experiment provide further evidence that individual differences in the truth effect are stable over time. We extended prior work in two important ways. First, we could demonstrate that reliable measurement of individual differences is achievable within a single session when the experimental design is optimized to do so, thereby validating previously derived recommendations (Zajdler & Schnuerch, 2026). Second, and critically, we extend prior evidence for the temporal stability of individual differences in the truth effect by showing that these differences are stable both across sessions and different retention intervals.

We find high signal-to-noise ratios and corresponding reliability in both tests with short retention intervals. This had a notable consequence for the analytical picture: the Pearson correlation of the observed truth-effect scores between these tests was already clearly detectable and showed only little attenuation relative to the model-based estimate.

This stands in contrast to what we observe in less reliable data. For example, the test after a one-week retention interval had a lower signal-to-noise ratio and consequently, Pearson correlations with scores from this test were also attenuated more compared to the model-based estimates. When reliability is high, the hierarchical model's ability to compensate for noisy data is less important, as the information is already present in the observed scores. This does not render the hierarchical approach superfluous, however. Its ability to quantify uncertainty through the posterior distribution remains a meaningful advantage over simple Pearson correlations, and we would advocate for its use as standard practice. But the present results make clear that the main practical levers for reliably detecting correlations are psychometric goodness and trial size, not modeling sophistication.

It is worth noting that, at the mean level, the truth effect does decrease with longer retention intervals (Henderson et al., 2021), and this pattern was replicated here. Crucially, however, this average decrease does not preclude stability at the individual level: individuals who showed larger truth effects after a short delay also tended to show larger effects after a longer delay. This suggests a stable component in individual susceptibility to the truth effect that persists over time, even as the average magnitude declines.

Taken together, these findings provide more definitive evidence for the stability of individual differences in the truth effect. By explicitly focusing on reliable measurement of individual effects and assessing stability both across sessions and retention intervals, we established that individual differences in the truth effect are stable over time and not largely determined by situational influences. This finding, together with the demonstration on how to reliably and efficiently measure individual truth effects, clears and guides the way for future research on how individual differences in the truth effect covary with dispositional variables.

General Discussion

We set out to establish whether the necessary prerequisites for research on individual differences in the truth effect are in place, specifically, whether individual differences can be reliably measured and whether they are stable over time. Across a reanalysis of three existing datasets and a new experiment, we have evidence that both prerequisites are met.

Individual differences in the truth effect are stable across different test sessions and, critically, across different retention intervals as well-a question that prior research had left largely unaddressed. Specifically, individual differences are stable when the same experimental procedure is repeated across sessions, as in Dataset 2 and our experiment, and when participants judge statements from an earlier exposure phase after a longer delay, as in Dataset 3 and our experiment. The finding that individual differences persist across different retention intervals strengthens the case for a stable component in individual susceptibility to the truth effect, rather than one that is highly sensitive to the specific timing of exposure and judgment.

We further demonstrate that individual differences in the truth effect can be reliably measured within a single experimental session, directly validating the design recommendations of Zajdler and Schnuerch (2026).

Prior work had suspected that multiple sessions might be necessary to achieve adequate reliability (De Keersmaecker et al., 2026); our results indicate that this reflects the psychometric properties of specific experimental designs rather than an inherent limitation of the truth-effect paradigm. Importantly, this is not to say that prior work was misguided. At the time, established guidelines for optimizing psychometric goodness in truth-effect studies were not yet available, and these studies represent important first steps. What the present findings add is a demonstration that truth-effect experiments can achieve high psychometric goodness and, with a sufficient number of trials per condition, high reliability within a single session. When the experimental design follows the recommendations of Zajdler and Schnuerch (2026) reliable individual-level truth effect scores are achievable without the need for repeated sessions. This has meaningful practical implications: single-session designs are substantially more cost-efficient and avoid the participant dropout that accompanies multi-session studies, considerably lowering the barrier for large-scale individual difference research on the truth effect.

A further observation is that, when psychometric goodness and reliability are high, correlations are well-detectable even with simpler analytical approaches. The Pearson correlations of observed truth-effect scores were already clearly localized in the more reliable data and significantly different from zero without requiring a hierarchical model analysis. This does not, however, render the hierarchical approach dispensable. Its key advantage lies in the ability to explicitly quantify uncertainty in the correlation estimates.

Where otherwise a non-significant point estimate might be misread as evidence for the null, Bayesian hierarchical models make plain when the data can tell us only little. This was especially visible in Dataset 1, a dataset with lower reliability, where a broad credible interval and a Bayes factor near 1 indicated that the data are simply too noisy to support any substantive conclusion. We therefore advocate for the use of hierarchical models as a general practice when assessing individual differences in the truth effect (see also Rouder, Yang, & Braver, 2026).

Limitations and Future Directions

One limitation of this study concerns the generalizability of the evidence we found for the stability of individual differences in the truth effect. We focused specifically on temporal stability, that is, whether individual differences in the truth effect persist across different time points and retention intervals. We could primarily examine retention intervals on the order of minutes within a single session, or, at most, one month between sessions. However, even these longer intervals may be short compared to real-world retention intervals, which may span several months or more between different encounters with the same claim. Future research should therefore extend the research on temporal stability to substantially longer retention intervals.

Stability, moreover, is a broader concept than persistence of individual differences over time alone. Individual differences might also be expected to generalize-or fail to generalize-across different item materials, content domains, or presentation modes (e.g., visual vs. auditory). Investigating further dimensions of stability therefore presents a promising and necessary avenue for future research on individual differences in the truth effect.

Finally, having established that individual differences in the truth effect are stable across sessions and can be reliably measured within a single session, it is now worthwhile to revisit their relationships with dispositional variables-a line of inquiry for which reliable (while cost-efficient) measurement and stable individual differences are a necessary prerequisite.

Conclusion

This research establishes the necessary prerequisites for grounded investigation of individual differences in the truth effect: reliable measurement and temporal stability.

Specifically, individual differences in the truth effect are stable across sessions and retention intervals, and can be reliably measured within a single experimental session. With these findings as a basis, the field is now well-positioned to revisit and extend investigations into how individual differences in the truth effect covary with stable dispositional variables such as personality traits and cognitive abilities-and, through this, to gain deeper insight into the mechanisms underlying the truth effect.

Appendix A Prior Specification

The priors on µ j , σ j , and Ω are specified in the main text, but the remaining model parameters require prior specifications as well. Priors on α, β, and τ² are set broadly and are specified hierarchically: with hyperpriors µ α ∼ Normal(0, 1), σ α ∼ Normal + (0, 1), µ β ∼ Normal(0, 1), and

Priors on all variance parameters are half-normals and bound by a lower value of 0 to ensure strictly positive values.

Appendix B Sensitivity Analysis

We assessed the sensitivity of our model results to prior specification by varying the priors of µ j , σ j , and Ω across a range of reasonable settings. The relevant priors are:

In the main analysis, we set a = 0.25, b = 0.25, and

For the sensitivity analysis, we varied these parameters across the following values: a ∈ {0.125, 0.25, 0.5}, b ∈ {0.125, 0.25, 0.5}, and η ∈ {0.5, 1, 2}.

Across all prior combinations, the pattern of Bayes factors remained consistent with the results reported in the main text, with no meaningful changes for the drawn conclusions.

Bayes factors for the stability model over the null model for each prior setting are provided in Table B1.

Appendix C Parameter Estimates

Posterior summaries for central model parameters are reported below for each dataset, for the models reported in the main text.

For Dataset 3, the bridge sampling algorithm did not converge when all four sessions were included, even though the MCMC posterior itself was well behaved. This may be because the estimated between-person variance of the truth effect in the last session was close to zero, that is, close to a boundary of the parameter space. We therefore re-estimated the model using only the first three sessions. Parameter estimates did not differ considerably between the three-and four-session models (see Tables C4 and C3).

Figure 1 provides a direct comparison of Pearson and model-based correlation estimates. The lower panel of Figure 2 shows the posterior distribution of the correlation alongside the Pearson correlation point estimate. In the upper panel, both the observed individual truth effects (M rep -M new , gray) and model estimates (θ, blue) are plotted for both sessions. Notably, the model estimates are distributed much closer around the mean and exhibit less variability than the observed scores. This effect is called shrinkage: In a hierarchical model, individual estimates are informed by data from all individuals to decrease unsystematic noise. Thus, when an individual's data are noisy, the model leans more on what it has learned from the group rather than trusting an individual's observed scores, pulling (or shrinking) that individual's estimate toward the average. Model comparison via Bayes factor did not favor one model over the other, BF10 = 0.61. These results reflect a lack of evidence in either direction rather than support for any particular structure of individual differences; the data simply do not afford the necessary precision for a clear verdict.

Dataset 2 Dataset

This dataset comes from Experiment 1 in DeKeersmaecker et al. (2026), where the goal was to establish the stability of individual differences in the truth effect. To that end, participants completed five sessions over 33 days. As inCalio et al. (2025), each session followed the same structure and sessions were spaced approximately one week apart. Each session consisted of an exposure phase, where participants rated how interesting they found 20 statements on a scale from 1 ("not interesting at all") to 6 ("very interesting"). In the following judgment phase, participants provided truth judgments on a scale from 1 ("definitely false") to 6 ("definitely true") for the 20 statements from the exposure phase and 20 novel statements. Importantly, each session contained different statements. Across sessions, truth effects decreased, but repeated statements consistently received higher truth judgments than novel statements, in the first session, M rep -M new = 0.32 (SD = 0.38), t(112) = 9.09, p < .001, Cohen's d = 0.86, the second session, M rep -M new = 0.21 (SD = 0.38), t(112) = 5.88, p < .001, Cohen's d = 0.55, the third session, M rep -M new = 0.18 (SD = 0.32), t(112) = 5.93, p < .001, Cohen's d = 0.56, the fourth session, M rep -M new = 0.15 (SD = 0.32), t(112) = 5.00, p < .001, Cohen's d = 0.47, and the fifth session, M rep -M new = 0.14 (SD = 0.31), t(112) = 4.62, p < .001, Cohen's d = 0.43. Beyond mean effects, these authors report that individual differences in the truth effect are reliable and stable and conclude that five sessions may be needed for reliable measurement.

The right column of Figure 4 shows the posterior distribution of the correlation alongside the Pearson correlation point estimates. The Pearson correlation is only mildly attenuated compared to the posterior mean. The posterior distributions are notably narrower than in Dataset 1, indicating substantially less uncertainty associated with the correlation estimates. In the left column of Figure 4, both the observed individual truth effects (M rep -M new , gray) and model estimates (θ, blue) are plotted for each paired combination of sessions. Compared to Dataset 1, there is considerably less shrinkage here: model-estimated effects are somewhat closer together than the observed scores, but the difference is small. This reflects the higher reliability associated with individual-level estimates in this dataset, as the model needs to rely less on group-level information for individual estimates.

Figure 4 Stability Results in Dataset 2

Figure 6 shows the posterior distribution of the correlation alongside the Pearson correlation point estimates. The Pearson correlations are attenuated compared to the posterior means. The posterior distributions are, in most cases, notably wider than in Dataset 2, indicating more uncertainty associated with these correlation estimates. The left column of Figure 6 plots both the observed individual truth effects (M rep -M new , gray) and model estimates (θ, blue) for each paired combination of sessions. As expected given the lower reliability in this dataset, shrinkage is more pronounced than in Dataset 2, though less so than in Dataset 1. The exceptions are Sessions 3 and 4, where model-based estimates are shrunk closely toward the group mean. This pattern likely reflects the lower and more variable reliability across sessions in this dataset.
